nameStory: The Long-tailed Jaeger gets its name from the dramatically long central tail feathers that stream behind it like ribbons in flight. 'Jaeger' comes from the German word for 'hunter,' reflecting this bird's aggressive pursuit of other seabirds to steal their food. It's also called a Long-tailed Skua, with 'skua' coming from the Faroese word for these piratical seabirds.
description: The Long-tailed Jaeger is a sleek, gull-like seabird that spends most of its life over the open ocean. About the size of a small gull, it's built for speed and agility with long, narrow wings and a distinctive streaming tail. These birds are aerial pirates, chasing other seabirds until they drop or regurgitate their catch, which the jaeger then snatches mid-air. In New England waters, they're rare visitors, usually seen during migration as they travel between their Arctic breeding grounds and southern wintering areas.

idTips.label: Streaming tail feathers
idTips.description: Two extremely long, narrow central tail feathers extend far beyond the rest of the tail, creating unmistakable streamers that flutter behind the bird like dark ribbons in flight

idTips.label: Flight style
idTips.description: Flies with light, buoyant wingbeats that look almost tern-like, with wings that appear narrow and pointed, creating a graceful, floating appearance over the waves

idTips.label: Overall coloring
idTips.description: Adults show clean gray-brown upperparts and white underparts with a distinctive dark cap on the head, while juveniles appear more uniformly brown with barred patterns

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more delicate than other jaegers, with a lighter, more refined appearance that makes it look almost falcon-like in flight

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen pursuing terns and small gulls in high-speed chases, twisting and turning with remarkable agility until the victim drops its fish

habitat: In New England, Long-tailed Jaegers are spotted over open ocean waters, usually several miles offshore where deep waters meet continental shelf areas. They're most often seen from whale-watching boats or during pelagic birding trips, rarely coming close to shore. When present, they favor areas where terns and other small seabirds are actively feeding, as these provide opportunities for their piratical lifestyle.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants may pass through in late May, usually far offshore and often mixed with flocks of other migrating seabirds.
seasonality.summer: Essentially absent from New England waters during summer months, as adults are busy breeding in the high Arctic tundra.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration occurs from late August through September, when both adults with their long tail streamers and brown juvenile birds may be spotted offshore.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter, as most birds have continued south to tropical and subtropical waters off South America and Africa.

funFact: Long-tailed Jaegers are incredible globe-trotters that make one of the longest migrations of any bird, traveling roughly 44,000 miles annually from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic feeding areas and back—equivalent to flying around the Earth nearly twice each year!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other jaegers, but the Long-tailed's streaming tail feathers are diagnostic when present. Juvenile birds without developed tail streamers can be tricky—look for their smaller size, lighter build, and more delicate flight style compared to the bulkier Parasitic and Pomarine Jaegers. Remember: 'Long-tailed = light and graceful.'
contextualKnowledge: The terms 'jaeger' and 'skua' refer to the same family of birds, with 'jaeger' typically used for the smaller, more migratory species and 'skua' for the larger, more robust ones. However, this same species is called Long-tailed Skua in Europe and Long-tailed Jaeger in North America, which can cause confusion when reading different field guides or birding reports.
compareHints: Among the three jaeger species found in New England waters, the Long-tailed is the smallest and most delicate, with the most pronounced tail streamers when adult. Parasitic Jaegers are bulkier with shorter tail projections, while Pomarine Jaegers are the largest and heaviest with distinctive twisted central tail feathers that look like spoons rather than streamers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Parasitic Jaegers are intermediate in size between the smaller Long-tailed Jaeger and the bulkier Pomarine Jaeger.
Pomarine Jaegers are the bulkiest of the three regular jaeger species in New England waters, noticeably stockier than the slender Long-tailed Jaeger and chunkier than the Parasitic Jaeger.
Unlike the smaller jaegers in its family, South Polar Skua has a much heavier build and shorter, squared tail rather than the elongated central tail feathers of adult jaegers.
Great Skuas are much larger and more robust than their jaeger relatives (Parasitic, Pomarine, and Long-tailed Jaegers).
